subject: design
source_evidence: Grounded in the skill body (Coverage, Philosophy of the skill, Verification, Do NOT Use When) and established generative-research practice (Portigal, Sharon, Beyer & Holtzblatt, Flanagan critical-incident technique, experience sampling).

cases.scenario: A PM hands the agent a draft interview script. Sample questions: 'Wouldn't it be great if the app reminded you to reorder?', 'Would you pay $10/month for that?', 'You find the current process frustrating, right?'
cases.context: The team wants to validate a reorder-reminder feature with five upcoming interviews.
cases.question: How should the agent review this script?
expected_flags: All three questions are leading and/or hypothetical/solution-prompting — they manufacture the expected answer
Replace with episodic questions: 'tell me about the last time you ran out of X' / 'walk me through how you reordered most recently'
Pricing/willingness-to-pay questions yield unreliable self-prediction, not evidence
Warn that a validating script will only confirm the team's prior belief
expected_fix_hints: Rewrite each question to be answerable by describing a concrete real past event
Use silence and 'say more about that' follow-ups instead of confirmation seeking
absent_signals: Do not keep the leading/hypothetical phrasing
Do not treat 'would you pay' answers as a demand signal

cases.scenario: A team wants to understand how ICU nurses actually use a new medication-charting tool during a shift, including the interruptions and workarounds they don't report.
cases.context: Nurses cannot stop work to be interviewed at length; behavior in the real environment matters.
cases.question: What research approach should the agent recommend?
expected_flags: Recommend a contextual/observational method (contextual inquiry or fly-on-the-wall observation) in the real environment
Observation outranks interview here because what people do and say they do differ — especially for unreported workarounds
Note the naturalism-vs-depth trade-off and choose minimal intrusion for a high-stakes workflow
Pair brief in-context clarifying questions (master-apprentice) rather than a long sit-down interview
expected_fix_hints: Shadow or observe on-shift with light contextual-inquiry questioning
Capture interruptions and workarounds as primary data, recorded with consent
absent_signals: Do not default to a conference-room interview removed from the real environment
Do not rely on nurses' after-the-fact recall of their own workarounds

cases.scenario: A team wants to learn how commuters' app usage shifts across a week — morning rush vs evening vs weekend — and a single interview keeps producing vague 'it depends' answers.
cases.context: The behavior varies day to day and is hard to recall accurately in one sitting.
cases.question: What should the agent propose?
expected_flags: Propose a diary study / experience sampling because the behavior unfolds over days and varies
In-the-moment capture (daily prompts, photo diary) reduces recall bias the single interview suffers from
Define a study window (e.g. one to two weeks) and prompt cadence
Synthesize the captured moments rather than relying on summarized memory
expected_fix_hints: Set up daily prompts capturing context at the moment of use
Recruit for variety across the relevant commuting patterns
absent_signals: Do not push for a longer single interview to fix the 'it depends' problem

cases.scenario: A founder asks the agent to 'go interview users and find out what we should build,' but the team has not agreed on which problem or which users they are studying.
cases.context: There is no shared problem statement; different stakeholders mean different user segments.
cases.question: How should the agent respond before designing the research?
expected_flags: Flag that the problem is not yet framed — research without a framed problem produces unfocused data
Route to problem-framing first, then design research to investigate the framed problem
Identify which users/segment the study targets and the recruitment criteria
Do not promise that interviews will hand over 'what to build' directly
expected_fix_hints: Run problem-framing to agree the question and the user segment
Then write an episodic interview guide scoped to that framed problem
absent_signals: Do not jump straight into interviews with an undefined target and goal

cases.scenario: A team recruited five power users who all loved the concept, and reports 'research validated the feature — everyone wants it.'
cases.context: All participants were existing enthusiasts recruited from the beta forum.
cases.question: How should the agent assess the rigor of this research?
expected_flags: Sample is biased — only enthusiasts; document who was excluded and why and recruit to match real criteria
If every finding confirms the prior belief, the questions were probably leading or the sample was self-selecting
A sound study should surface at least one finding that contradicts the team's going-in hypothesis
'Everyone wants it' from five hand-picked fans is not validation
expected_fix_hints: Recruit a sample that matches the target criteria, including non-enthusiasts
Audit the guide for leading questions and re-run with neutral, episodic prompts
absent_signals: Do not accept enthusiast consensus as feature validation
Do not skip documenting sample composition and exclusions

cases.scenario: A growth lead asks the user-research owner to interpret last quarter's NPS survey results, classify which inbound agent requests are high-risk, and set up an A/B test of two onboarding flows.
cases.context: The team conflates 'research' with all data and measurement work.
cases.question: How should the agent scope these requests?
expected_flags: NPS/survey interpretation is quantitative analytics — out of scope for generative qualitative research
Classifying agent requests by risk is agent-side intent classification — out of scope; not human research at all
A/B test of onboarding flows is experimental evaluation with a control group — out of scope (use experimental methods)
Offer the in-scope adjacent value: generative interviews/observation to learn why users behave as the metrics suggest
expected_fix_hints: Redirect each request to its proper practice (analytics, intent classification, experimentation)
Propose qualitative research only where the question is 'why/what do users do and need'
absent_signals: Do not interpret survey statistics as a user-research deliverable
Do not design an A/B test or risk classifier under the user-research banner

cases.scenario: Watching a recording, the agent sees the interviewer finishing the participant's sentences, jumping in with 'so basically you mean X?', and filling every pause.
cases.context: The team wants feedback on interviewing technique before the next sessions.
cases.question: What technique corrections should the agent give?
expected_flags: Stop finishing sentences and paraphrasing — it imposes the interviewer's framing on the participant's account
Leave silence intact; use it as a tool to let the participant continue
Replace 'so you mean X?' with neutral 'say more about that' / 'tell me what happened next'
Treat surprising answers as signal of new information rather than something to reconcile to a hypothesis
expected_fix_hints: Practice tolerating pauses and using open follow-ups
Record and review to catch confirmation-seeking and interruption habits
absent_signals: Do not coach the interviewer to confirm their own hypothesis faster
